answer.rationale: The binding constraints eliminate most directions: the incumbent has refused to reopen price, so negotiate_terms (memory_c4) and renew_incumbent (memory_c1, memory_c6) cannot satisfy the 18% mandate; the contract expires in 14 days without auto-renew, so defer_decision (memory_c5) risks a supply gap unless a month-to-month bridge is actually available; add_second_source (memory_c3) addresses concentration risk but does not by itself replace expiring primary volume or hit the mandate. That leaves switching primary supply to the low-cost vendor, which memory_c2 says worked before. But memory_c2 is exactly the load-bearing claim, and it is thin in a telling way: it attests to unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy \u2014 not to on-time delivery at sustained committed volume. At 94% utilization with no buffer, delivery reliability is the only failure mode that matters, and the memory is silent on it. So I want the archived source for memory_c2 to see whether that prior switch was at comparable volume and criticality, and whether delivery performance was measured at all or simply not recorded. I intend the switch as a phased transition, not a wholesale cutover: qualify and ramp the low-cost vendor on the volume needed to hit the mandate while holding the incumbent on short-term or month-to-month terms for the balance as long as that is obtainable, so a first-cycle miss does not stop the line. If the archive shows memory_c2 covered only a low-volume, non-constrained part, I would downgrade to a bridge extension plus qualification and accept partial mandate attainment this cycle rather than put committed volume at risk. Residual risk flagged: cost savings here are realized immediately and visibly while delivery degradation surfaces later, which biases the record toward crediting the switch; also, a full switch trades one single point of failure for another, undoing the concentration lesson in memory_c3.
